inline.s: The Eighteenth Year, Gengyin ●

I was forty-five. That spring I wrote out the Lotus Sutra in gratitude to the Sacred Mother. At that time certain men who coveted our practice site suborned a Daoist priest from beyond the pale, falsely claiming that he held that temple, and gathered a crowd to lodge a suit at the governor's yamen. Lord Li, the provincial governor, had already learned the whole affair and bitterly hated it; he sent it down to Laizhou prefecture for a thorough investigation. I attended the hearing in person and did my utmost to save them. Several hundred of those ruffians raised an uproar in the prefectural city, surrounding us as the men of Kuang once surrounded Confucius. I had two attendants with me; I sent them off by another road and walked slowly on alone. The leader among them came capering at me with a blade, meaning to kill me. I looked at him with a smile and said: 'If you kill a man, how will you answer for yourself?' His spirit failed him, he put up his sword, and they escorted me about two li beyond the city wall. When we were about to part, the mad crowd suspected their leader of having been won over to my side and wanted to beat him. I reckoned silently: if that crowd once rouses itself, the man is lost. What was to be done? I hesitated. At the parting I drew the madman with me to my lodging, shut the door, took off my robe, sat at ease, laughed and talked as usual, and shared melons and fruit with him. Meanwhile the whole market was crying that a Daoist had killed a monk. The prefect heard it and at once sent many runners to arrest them all. The crowd was terrified and all knocked their heads on the ground, begging to be let off. I said: 'Do not be afraid; only hear what I have to say, that is all.' When they arrived, the prefect asked: 'Did the mad ruffians kill the monk?' I said: 'Not at all. When the arrest came, the monk was eating melons and fruit together with their leader.' The prefect said: 'Why did they raise the uproar?' I said: 'It was mere market noise.' The prefect wanted to put them in the cangue. I said: 'You wish to disperse them; the cangue would only hold them fast.' The prefect understood, and ordered the local officers to drive them all out. Within three days the whole mad crowd had dispersed, and so the matter was quieted. That year I wrote A Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi. (The Sacred Mother appeared seven times; Lord Li the provincial governor and the Laizhou prefect, once each.)

Zheng observes: in this affair of strife, every step is the art of war and every step a Chan device. Were it so, there would be no difficult affair under heaven and no man hard to deal with. Among the eight essays of A Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, only the essay On the Dharma of Mind is short in written extent yet comprehensive in its treatment of the Three Teachings; I append it here to preserve its general outline. On the Dharma of Mind it says: In youth I took Confucius as my teacher and did not know Confucius; I took Laozi as my teacher and did not know Laozi. Then I withdrew into the deep mountains and great marshes, practicing stillness and contemplating the mind. From this I came to know that the three realms are mind only and the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only. Once one contemplates mind and consciousness thus, all forms are the shadows of the mind and all sounds are the echoes of the mind. It follows that all sages are the source of those shadows, and all teachings are the echo that follows the sound. Because the ten thousand dharmas are manifested by mind alone, the words of statesmanship and the pursuits of livelihood all accord with the true Dharma. Because outside the mind there is no dharma, every dharma is real. The deluded cling to them and so fail of the wonder (variant reading: 'awaken'); but if one awakens to one's own mind, no dharma is other than wondrous. That both mind and dharmas should be wondrous, only a sage can attain. When Hanshan wrote these eight essays he happened to be just then resolving the trouble with the Daoists; was this not also an allegory of harmonizing the Three Teachings? No wonder the Daoists bore him no grudge.
The Nineteenth Year, Xinmao ●

I was forty-six. That year the Sacred Mother had a sandalwood Vairocana Buddha image made, and the great hall was completed. In autumn my disciple Huang Ziguang passed away seated in meditation. (The Sacred Mother appeared eight times; Huang Ziguang, a second time.)
Zheng remarks: this is a deep approbation of Ziguang, and the special mention echoes the affair of the jichou year; it is the brush method of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The Twentieth Year, Renchen ●

I was forty-seven. In the seventh month of autumn I went to the capital and visited Master Daguan at Shangfang. In the Jin dynasty there had been Master Wan, who, fearing that the three calamities would destroy the kalpa and leave no Buddhadharma, carved the sutras in stone and stored them in stone chambers. His stupa court had been sold off by monks; the master redeemed it and wished me to come and write its record. I arrived just then, and the master was overjoyed. As soon as we met we went together to Stone Sutra Mountain, and I composed the Record of Master Wan's Stupa Court and the Record of the Re-consecration of the Relics, together with the earlier Haiyin Draft. At that time I sat face to face with Master Da and lingered forty days and nights, the wonder of my life. (Master Daguan, a second time.)

Zheng's note: In Fangshan county there are stone sutra caves. In the Sui dynasty Master Jingwan hewed stone into slabs, carved a whole canon of sutras, stored them in the caves, and sealed them with stone doors; in successive ages all left stele inscriptions. After Master Da took the place in hand, a monk named Zinan of Shideng Hermitage in the capital raised funds to continue the carving. This was in the wuwu year of Wanli, when Zheng was in the capital sitting for the classics examination and did his utmost to help the work. I have also heard it from an attendant of Wuru: that in the renchen year the two masters met in a garden in the western suburbs of the capital and sat facing each other, forty days and nights without closing their eyes, planning to compile a Transmission of the Lamp for the Ming dynasty, and therefore agreed to go and dredge Caoxi to open the Dharma lineage, and so on. Here he says only that it was 'the wonder of my life' and does not elaborate; perhaps this was not wonderful enough, and there was something more extraordinary still.
The Twenty-First Year, Guisi ●

I was forty-eight. That year Shandong suffered a great famine, and the starving dead lay along the roads. All the provisions stored in the mountain I gave out to relieve the people near the mountain; when that was not enough, I took passage on a convenient boat to Liaodong and bought several hundred piculs of beans to succor them. In this way, among the people of the four communities of the border mountains, not one starved to death.

Reading to this point, Zheng sighs that the karmic affinity of Haiyin at Laoshan was thus hastily concluded. Yet in the twelve years from first to last, his transforming activity and his universal relief were already within inconceivable merit.
The Twenty-Second Year, Jiawu ●

I was forty-nine. In the third month of spring Lord Zheng Kunya, provincial governor of Shandong, came into the mountains to visit and ask about the Dharma, and I spoke to him words of skillful means. In the tenth month of winter I went to court to offer congratulations on the imperial birthday festival, and stayed in the capital through the new year. I was invited to expound the precepts at Cishou Temple. At that time, because of the karmic conditions for restoring our own temple, and knowing that the Sacred Mother's reserves were already ample, I petitioned to begin the work. But as the emperor was then deliberating a punitive expedition against the Japanese who had invaded Korea, it was put off for the time being and the matter was laid aside. (The Sacred Mother appeared nine times; the emperor, five times; Governor Zheng Kunya, once.)

Zheng's note: 'Going to court to offer congratulations on the sacred festival' refers to the winter solstice festival and congratulations to the Sacred Mother, not to the emperor; the text afterwards uses 'the emperor' specially to distinguish them. The Sacred Mother's invitation to expound the precepts at Cishou Temple closed the case of the Great Cishou Temple built in the capital in the jimao year. The karmic conditions for restoring Bao'en, our own temple — the Sacred Mother's reserves were already ample and the affair was nearly accomplished, yet the conditions were laid aside and it was not completed — closed the case of his earlier northern journey and his original vow to revive that temple. Such is the brush method of the Spring and Autumn Annals, which introduces a matter at its beginning and concludes it at its end. Had it not been for restoring the temple, he would not have gone to offer congratulations and stayed in the capital. Had he not come and gone to the capital for three years, he would not have been drawn into the deliberations and incurred calamity. I have heard from an attendant of the Zongjing Hall in those days that when the Sacred Mother invited him to expound the precepts, the ceremonial gifts were exceedingly lavish. Cishou Temple was also called Shangfang Tushita Court; the abbot's quarters were spread with felt and brocade, and the fruit and food offered to the Buddha were all rare things from the four quarters. The robes, food, and vessels required by the abbot's quarters were sent by the Grand Master of Ceremonies, streaming to and fro along the road morning and evening, and onlookers were always packed like a wall. The offerings of nobles and imperial relatives and of the palace eunuchs could not be reckoned. Children who rejoiced in the merit all received a share of it. Of the money and grain from the inner treasury that were bestowed, he accepted not a fraction; he took only the alms bowls of the fifty-three pilgrims of the fifty-three visits. In one day the bowls all came back empty, yet gold and coins, cloth and grain had already filled the boxes and overflowed the granaries. Thousands of people gathered around him daily, and none failed to be fully fed from the fragrant kitchen. On the eighth day of the twelfth month that year, the Sacred Mother specially commanded her attendant Chen Ru to bestow a Vairocana hat, a brocade purple kashaya, Zhigong shoes, and undergarments, all of thick velvet; Hanshan declined them all, and only at the third bestowal did he accept them, and having accepted them he still did not wear them. At that time Master Daguan was living at Stone Sutra Mountain. When the stone chamber was opened, a casket was found beneath the Buddha's seat, containing countless Buddha relics. When the Sacred Mother heard of it she likewise sent attendants with offerings of vegetarian food and bestowed a purple kashaya, made great offerings to the relics for three days, and had them re-consecrated in the stone cave. Master Da wrote a memorial declining the gift and yielding it to Master Hanshan. His verse says: These thirty years on rivers and seas I have gone, / in a single patched robe I have watched the seasons run. / Ashamed, this poor frame scarce can wear the purple bright; / I turn and give it to a loftier man, whose merit shines more light. This was because Hanshan was still in the capital and would not wear it; Master Da therefore also refused it, wishing to yield it to Hanshan and have him wear it, and so he said 'his merit shines more light.' On the day the robes were bestowed, the Sacred Mother commanded an attendant to convey her decree that he be invited into the palace so that she might ask him face to face for a Dharma name. The master knew this was not the emperor's wish and firmly declined, saying that by ancestral rule monks do not enter the palace; so attendants were sent to paint his portrait, and he gave a name which was presented. The Sacred Mother hung the portrait in an inner hall, made the emperor stand in attendance, and bowed to receive the Dharma name. The emperor served the Sacred Mother with the utmost filial piety, and on that day he could not keep his countenance from changing. The Sacred Mother's Dharma name is recorded later in the chronicle. In the Dharma lineage's forty-character verse, 'virtue, great, fortune, deep, vast,' the second character, 'great,' served as her name character. When the name was given and brought into the palace, the attendants never got to hear it. But from then on the 'great' generation was avoided, and all his Dharma heirs began with the 'fortune' generation. At that time the Sacred Mother's reserves for building the temple were ample, and this was but a casual surpassing cause. Had the inner treasury accounts been examined and the reserves traced to his hand, he would have had no way to clear himself, and how could he have escaped calamity? Fortunately the affair was laid aside and no donated funds were involved. He gave thanks for the favor and set out for home; he met with calamity but came to no harm. And so I reflect that the Bowl Inscription of those days — a vessel that makes light of ten thousand piculs — and the Robe Inscription — a garment that makes light of all under heaven — are here greatly borne out; how could they be empty words?
The above closes the three public cases: Laoshan, Cishou, and the vow to revive this temple.
The Twenty-Third Year, Yiwei ●

I was fifty. In the second month of spring I returned from the capital to the coast, and at once met with calamity. It began with the imperial gift of the canon: an inner envoy had been sent to escort it back. Earlier the emperor had always disliked the inner envoys for petitioning too often for funds for Buddhist works. When one of them reached the Eastern Sea, the palace happened to provoke the imperial wrath over some other matter, which threatened to reach those about the Sacred Mother, and the great ministers feared for them. Just then a powerful favorite at court who begrudged the envoy who had brought the sutras and wished him dead seized the occasion to start trouble. He made use of the earlier rumors spread by the Daoists and had a runner of the Eastern Depot (the secret police of the Ming) dress as a Daoist and beat the petition drum to present an accusation. When the emperor read it he was furious and ordered an arrest, and because of the sutra-escort affair I too was implicated. When I heard the news I gathered the assembly and said: 'The Buddha, for the sake of one being, does not forsake the three evil paths. This Eastern Sea is a mleccha land, where the very names of the Three Jewels were never heard. Now I have taught and transformed it for twelve years, and even three-year-old children all know to recite the Buddha's name. As for those who have abandoned the false and returned to the true, whole villages and households have done so. My vow is fulfilled; what regret should I have in dying? Only that my vow to restore this temple remains unaccomplished — that alone pains my heart.' When I left Jimo, the scholars and common people of the city, old and young, saw me off in tears — enough to show how men's hearts had been moved. When I reached the capital I was ordered to the Zhenfu Judicial Office for interrogation. The officials there had first received a hint of the imperial will (that is, the sovereign's intention) and wanted me to confess everything and trace out all the funds the Sacred Mother had donated to the various famous mountains, which would have amounted to no less than several hundred thousand. Under severe torture I said: 'I am ashamed that as a monk I have no way to repay the nation's grace. How should I now begrudge one death and so wound the emperor's great filial piety? To twist the truth and make false confessions in order to seize profit, and to obey the imperial will in a way that damages the cardinal bonds of morality, is by no means how a subject loves his lord. What would the historians say?' I resisted with all my might, even at the cost of death, and confessed only to more than seven hundred taels given by former benefactors, asking that the emperor examine the inner treasury accounts. When they were examined, apart from earlier famine relief there was indeed no record, and so the imperial displeasure dissolved, and mother and son were as before. In the end, by the emperor's gracious commiseration, I was sentenced for privately founding a monastery and sent into exile at Leizhou. When I was imprisoned in the third month of that year, all the temples of the capital chanted sutras and performed repentance rites for my protection. Among the monks there were those who burned incense on their arms and recited spells to add their protection. The son of Zheng Fanxi, Grand Marshal of Ansu, then in the Imperial Guard, though we had never met, specially held a banquet and gathered the officials at court to plead for me, even to weeping, protesting my innocence — none but grieved for the Dharma gate. Thus one sees how at that time men's hearts stood for the Dharma. I was in prison eight months, and the only one who brought me supplies was my attendant Fushan. In the tenth month of winter I was sent south. Many of the court's scholar-officials, in plain clothes and on ponies, escorted me and helped me across the fords. On the day I left the capital, my attendant Fushan and two or three monks went with me. In the eleventh month I reached Nanjing and took leave of my aged mother by the river; I wrote the Mother and Son Inscription and took my orphaned nephew Kejiu along. Earlier, when I had crossed Stone Sutra Mountain with Master Daguan, the thought came to us that the Chan gate was desolate; we said that Caoxi is the source, and the source must be choked, and so we vowed to go together and dredge it. My affairs prevented it, and Master Da went ahead, waiting for me at Mount Kuang. When I met with calamity the master was living at Tianchi. Hearing the report he was greatly shocked and said: 'If Master Hanshan is finished, then the vow for Caoxi remains unfulfilled.' He went first to Caoxi, then to the capital to report on my behalf. He hurried to and fro, and on his way back at Liaocheng he heard that I was soon to be released, and so returned to Jinling to wait. When I arrived we took leave of each other at the Traveler's Lodge by the river. The master wished to strive to clear me of the false charge. I said: 'The command of lord and father is the business of subject and son; there is no difference. And is it not settled karma? I beg you, master, say no more.' At the parting he grasped my arm and said: 'When I heard at Tianchi of your trouble, I at once vowed before the Buddha to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times to keep you from harm. My mind is your tongue.' I assented and took my leave; the master wrote A Discourse on Expelling the Guest and gave it to me in farewell. (The Sacred Mother appeared ten times; the emperor, six times; the son of Grand Marshal Zheng Fanxi of the Imperial Guard, once; the attendant Fushan, a second time; my aged mother, ten times; Master Daguan, three times.)

Zheng's note: In the yiwei year the crown prince was fourteen years old, yet the succession was still unsettled and court opinion was in confusion. The Sacred Mother favored Taichang and the proposal to establish the eldest; the emperor favored the Prince of Fu and the proposal to establish the son of highest rank. Of the inner court attendants, nine in ten sided with Consort Zheng, and the powerful men of the outer court echoed them, so that the foundation of the state was nearly shaken. Those who mediated in the midst of it advocated the theory of enfeoffing the three princes together. Those who stood firm — such as the Grand Secretary Zhang Weihongyang, the Grand Secretary Wang Jiaping, the supervising secretary Zou Yuanbiao (Nangao), and the ministry official Gao Panlong (Jingyi) — were no more than a few men. Taichang was moreover often ill, and the heir apparent had not won the emperor's heart; it was a moment of perilous, crosswise tension. Those who understood the matter said that the prayers for an heir at Wutai and the protection of the heir at Cishou, involving a man who had left the world in affairs so weighty for the dynasty's fate, put Hanshan in great danger. Originally one prayer had been at Wudang and one at Wutai, and so the Sacred Mother ended with Wutai and the emperor ended with Wudang. Treacherous men within and without watched for the emperor's momentary moods, and had the Eastern Depot runner disguise himself as a Daoist, using shadows and echoes to seize a pretext, in order to topple the monk by stripping the branches and pulling out the root. That day it truly became a prairie fire — yet it had nothing whatever to do with the Daoists of Laoshan. It was only that the Daoists left no trace, and one knows the palace was in a great tempest. Hanshan had first come to the court's notice through the karmic cause of praying for and obtaining an heir at Wutai, which had already become a seed of disaster. Because he avoided fame, within half a year he withdrew into hiding and escaped. Now, because of the reserves laid up for Bao'en, he could not forget the capital; he came and went, lingering nearly three years, and so the great crux and the great right-and-wrong of establishing the heir swept him into its wake. Moreover, his request that the Sacred Mother reduce her table by a hundred taels a day and accumulate reserves for three years greatly inconvenienced the inner officials, and so rifts easily arose. And since by ancestral rule the empress dowager might not interfere in court politics, it was natural that for a time those within and without should seize the pretext to attack him. Long ago the Second Patriarch calmly accepted wrongdoing, and those who knew the truth called it repaying a debt; was not this a repaying of debt, and a vast one? In the prison record, the single phrase 'to obey the imperial will in a way that damages the cardinal bonds of morality is by no means how a subject loves his lord' weighs as much as a nine-tripod cauldron. The words 'cardinal bonds' — were they uttered merely over donated funds? The Haiyin Temple took its name from the Sacred Mother's decree; no imperial edict had been sought, and so he was charged with privately founding it. Here it does not say the temple was destroyed; but in the stupa inscription for Master Da, the preface says plainly that the temple was destroyed. Alas! The sentencing officer's application of the law was excessive; what of filial devotion? This account of taking leave of his mother I will not elaborate again — in the end it is a mother letting go of her son; the eight words 'taking leave of his aged mother by the river at Nanjing' suffice to close one great public case of serving one's parents. The preface to the Mother and Son Inscription gives the details; I append it.

Qing, having brought trouble on himself by spreading the Dharma, provoked the wrath of the sage emperor, whose voice was like thunder. I thought privately of my aged mother: hearing of it she must have been frightened to death. Yet by grace I was spared death and sent into exile at Leiyang. Passing through my native place, I welcomed my aged mother to a meeting by the river; she was joyful, laughing and talking, her voice clear and bright, and in her breast there was not the slightest trace of a stagnant thought. So I asked her: when you, old mother, heard that your son stood between death and life, were you not anxious? My mother said: 'Death and life are allotted; I myself am not anxious, so why should I be anxious for you? It is only that people's talk is confused, and I had no settled view of the matter, and so I doubted.' We sat together in attendance on one another until dawn, and then made our final parting. My aged mother instructed me: 'Take good care of yourself in the Way, and do not be anxious on my account; now I take my long farewell of you.' She went gladly on her way without once looking back. And so I was moved that there are mothers under heaven such as this — does she not in a flash exhaust the feelings of birth and death? Therefore I made this inscription for her: The love of mother and son / is a lodestone drawing a needle; / the wondrous nature, naturally so, / is from the first complete. / I see my mother / as fire comes forth from wood: / the wood is burned away, / the fire in truth is not-self. / Living, I did not cling; / dying, as if unknowing. / Only then do I see this body / is a barren woman's child.

Appended: while in the prison I read the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. On the chapter of the Four Marks it says: Bells and drums, gongs and cymbals never cease their sound; voice upon voice by day and night preaches the Unborn. Pitiful are those who, drunk in dreams, wound their own lives — gazing at each other in a mirror, tears come pouring down. (The mark of self.) Jutting, jagged peaks rear up an iron city; forests of knives and trees of swords, cold as ice. Who knows that fire breaks out from the ice mountain? The ice mountain is burned away, the fire is not born. (The mark of man.) The iron gate is barred fast, deep and hard to open; lock upon lock — how bitter it is! Strange are the guests who groan through the long night, not knowing for what they came into this. (The mark of beings.) One bloody staff, utterly pitiless; touch it and it must cut off birth and death. When the pain reaches the heart and stings the nose, then you know the king's law is perfectly clear. (The mark of a life span.)

Coming out of the prison, I passed through the market of Chang'an; four verses: The wind and moon of Chang'an are the same in every age; on purple paths and red dust the road never ends. Most of all it is where one is called most intimately — a single cock-crow, the bell at the fifth watch. The body, like empty space, is at ease of itself; not a speck of dust divides the ten thousandfold mountains. Pitiful, the travelers in the bright sun and blue sky, eyes wide open, sighing that the road is hard. A squall and sudden rain come in a moment; countless travelers cannot open their eyes. Then of a sudden the rain stops, the clouds scatter away — the great void was from the first beyond all dust. Men of the mirage city in the air, the shimmering dust; before the eyes they seem like a village in mist. You must walk right into the city and look: sound and form from the first were never real.
In that year the Caoxi karmic affinity began.

blocks.text: A Commentary on the Autobiographical Chronicle of Elder Hanshan (Volume Two)

inline.s: The Twenty-Fourth Year, Bingshen ●

I was fifty-one. In the first month of spring I passed through Wenjiang and visited Supervising Secretary Zou. Wang Xinghai, a grand herald of Luling, paid me homage on the river and asked me to annotate the Lankavatara. In the second month I crossed the Dayu Range; at the ridge I looked at the place where Huiming seized the robe and wrote a poem in remembrance. It has the lines: Turning it over, I think of the traveler who walked by night — how does it compare with my heart crossing the ridge today? Seeing the travelers sweating blood, I instructed one monk to found a tea-giving hermitage at the ridge. Seeing the road rugged and hard to travel, I had the Daoist laymen urge its repair, and within a few years it became a level highway. Reaching Shaoyang, I entered the mountain to pay homage to the Patriarch. Drinking the water of Caoxi, I made this verse: A drop of Caoxi's water from the spirit source / flows into the vast sea, waves beating the sky. / How many fish and dragons have transformed therein — / yet the single vein at the source is still cool and clear. Seeing the ancestral court in decline beyond words, I departed sorrowing. Arriving at Wuyang in prison garb, I met the Grand General, who loosed my bonds, entertained me with a vegetarian meal, and lodged me at Haizhu Temple. At that time the grand counselor Zhou Dingshi was expounding Wang Yangming's teaching, and brought several dozen of his disciples to visit. In the course of the conversation Zhou raised the phrase 'comprehending the way of day and night' and posed it as a question. Among the company there was one called the Old Daoist Elder, who answered: 'Everyone has awareness: when matters are met by day, it is this awareness; when dreaming at night, it is also this awareness; therefore it is said, comprehending the way of day and night.' Zhou said: 'That is how everyone explains it, but in my heart I am not so sure.' Then he asked me: 'Old Chan master, pray instruct us.' I said: 'From what classic does this saying come?' He said: 'The Appended Remarks of the Book of Changes,' and recited several lines in succession. I said: 'This is the Sage pointing out to people that they must awaken to that which does not belong to birth and death.' Zhou clapped his hands and said: 'Truly the old Chan master's instruction is intimate and to the point.' The company was all bewildered. When they asked again, Zhou said: 'Birth and death are the way of day and night; to comprehend day and night is to no longer belong to day and night.' The whole assembly sighed in admiration. Earlier, the various protectors of the Dharma had written to the supreme commander Grand Marshal Chen, who sent post-horses to ferry me along. On the tenth day of the third month I reached Leizhou, was enrolled in the garrison, and lodged in an old temple west of the city. On the first day of the fourth month, summer, I began to annotate the Lankavatara Sutra. That year there was a great famine and pestilence broke out everywhere; no rain fell for a whole year, and the dead and injured were beyond telling. I sat as if in a charnel grove, yet by the power of the Dharma I was at ease. As the drought went on the well water dried up; only the attendant Shan remained with me. Each midnight we would get one jar of water to last the day; to the starving, a single drop was like heavenly nectar. Inside and outside the city the accumulated bones lay exposed. In the seventh month of autumn I and the provincial graduate Ke Shifu urged the people to gather and bury the bones, which numbered by the ten thousand. Then I held a rite for their deliverance, and at once it rained heavily, water three feet deep on level ground, and from then on the pestilential air lifted. In the eighth month the garrison headquarters summoned me back to Wuyang; I lodged at the military drill ground, and coming and going wrote twenty poems In the Army. Earlier, passing the Bitter Vine of Dianbai, the gateway of the mountain road, I composed an inscription and founded a tea-giving hermitage. Ding Youwu, grand counselor of Yuzhang, was exiled to the Guang sea on a false charge; when he arrived, having long admired me, we became fast friends. (Wenjiang's Supervising Secretary Zou; Wang Xinghai, grand herald of Luling; the Grand General, whose surname is unknown; Grand Counselor Zhou Dingshi; Grand Marshal Chen of the supreme command; the provincial graduate Ke Shifu; Grand Counselor Ding Youwu — once each. The attendant Shan is Fushan — three times. Supervising Secretary Zou was named Yuanbiao, styled Nangao, a native of Jishui in Jiangxi; he passed the metropolitan examination in the dingchou year of Wanli. He it was who at court censured Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng for remaining in office during mourning, and was exiled for seven years; he was later recalled to the Ministry of Personnel and rose to Left Censor-in-Chief. Zhou Dingshi was the later Haimen, named Rudeng, styled Jiyuan, a native of Shengxian in Zhejiang. Lord Chen was named Dake, styled Sijin, a native of Yangzhou.)

Zheng observes: before Hanshan ever went up Wutai, he first entered Shaolin to pay homage to the First Patriarch. Here, before reaching Leizhou, he first entered Caoxi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch. Dharma affinity is host; worldly affinity is guest. No Dharma affinity is too great: wherever he goes he visits the Patriarch and annotates sutras. No Dharma affinity is too small: everywhere he gives tea and buries bones.
The Twenty-Fifth Year, Dingyou ●

I was fifty-two. In the first month of spring, as there were many dead and wounded in the provincial city and bones lay exposed, I had people gather and bury them, also several thousand in number, and held a Universal Relief rite for seven days and nights, with Ding Youwu himself assisting. Before this the Cantonese did not know the Buddha; from this time on they turned to him as one. In the fourth month of summer the Lankavatara Notes were finished; and because some of the scholars who had taken refuge lacked an entry into Buddhist principle, I wrote Straight Pointers to the Doctrine of the Mean to draw them out. At first high and low alike, seeing me to be a condemned monk, made very light of me. At that time the supreme commander Grand Marshal Lord Chen Rugang enforced the law most strictly, and none dared visit him privately. Earlier, because someone had spoken of me, though I had not gone to see him, he sent people to inquire after me most assiduously. In the ninth month of that year I went with Youwu to call on him; when we reached his gate the runners reported us and we were turned away. On our return, that very evening he came in person to pay his respects to me on my boat, bringing tea and food, and sat talking until the third watch, to everyone's astonishment. Afterwards he spoke of me to all the authorities in the highest terms, saying: 'He is a qilin and phoenix among monks,' and instructed the three provincial offices to go and pay him homage. From then on all Lingnan knew that monks were to be honored. (Ding Youwu and Lord Chen Rugang each appear a second time.)

Zheng records that the Outer Record of Hanshan says: when he first came to visit a certain garrison commander, he held his card below the steps, and for a long while was not told to rise and withdraw. He understood in his heart: should I not announce my own name and present myself? Yet he could not get the words out of his mouth; they weighed on him like a thousand catties, and there was nothing to be done. Then he summoned his courage, gave his own name, and announced himself, and only then was he allowed to rise and withdraw. The next day at the audience it was the same; for a whole year there was no respite. Others said: how should a military man know to break convention in dealing with a man of knowledge? At the last, on a day when they were to visit the governor together, the commander prepared a boat stocked with vegetarian food and fruit like a banquet for guests, invited him aboard, bowed and saluted him to the seat of honor, and said: 'It is not that I could not have made an exception for you; I knew you had proud bones, and so I did but help you along.' They talked happily knee to knee before parting. And so one sighs that among magistrates there are many men of deep feeling — why ask about a mere military officer? Zheng suspects that this affair, had it occurred before Lord Chen Rugang's condescension, would be a different matter; but in the days of Rugang and Youwu it was still the manner of a military officer. I have heard that in those days in the ranks he was known as Cai Deqing; he let his hair grow and kept a long beard, and at leisure wore the Dongpo cap. From the day of his exile at fifty until his sixty-ninth year, he then shaved before the Sacred Mother's spirit tablet, removed beard and hair, and returned to the monk's robes. The Outer Record also says: while in Lingnan the people were not yet familiar with him, and he kept a lofty reserve, so that he could not put people at ease and had no one close to him. There was a little child who wanted to come near him but was always afraid and ran off. One day, learning the lion's way of taming its cub, he forced himself to lie down and be playful with the child and gave him fruits; day by day the child grew more familiar and no longer feared him. From then on people no longer shunned him but came daily to be near him. Zheng knows that this thought of the perfected man treating the world as a child comes from the power of Laozi — the saying that all under heaven are infants, and I too am an infant with them. And our Confucian benevolence and my Buddha's compassion do not depart from this either.
The Twenty-Sixth Year, Wuxu ●

I was fifty-three. In the first month of spring the censor Lord Fan Youxuan, for his stand on establishing the heir, was exiled to Leiyang. He first visited me at Wuyang while I was collating the Lankavatara draft, and asked me what the scenery of Leiyang was like. I picked up a scroll of the sutra and showed it to him, saying: 'This is the scenery of Leiyang.' He marveled and at once wrote a petition to raise funds for its printing. When Lord Zhou Haimen held the post of salt intendant in Guangdong he came and went asking after the Way, and as he also had charge of Nan-Shao he asked me to compile a Gazetteer of Caoxi. The scholars of Guangdong had until then not known the Buddha; it happened that Lord Zhou was expounding Wang Yangming's teaching and had gathered the scholars to ask me about the Way. There was a certain Long Zhang who, hearing my discourse, was struck by it in his heart; he went home and told his friends Wang Anshun and Feng Changli: 'The Chan master who has come from the north preaches a most wonderful Dharma.' The two came to ask for instruction, and when I revealed to them the matter of the upward path they believed firmly without doubt and set their minds earnestly on investigation. These two men had long been of virtuous conduct, and those who came one after another to take refuge in the Dharma gate grew daily more numerous; from this time they first knew that there are Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Thereafter the Dharma teaching opened wide, and it was the strength of these three men. I often recalled Master Da's vow concerning the sutra and had no convenient way to repay it. That summer I first built a Chan hut among the ramparts, intending to follow Dahui's example of teaching the Dharma to those in caps and kerchiefs. So I gathered the disciples who had long relied on me from afar — Xingrong, Rugan, and others — and the disciples beneath the bodhi tree of Dharmata — Tong'an, Chaoyi, and others — several dozen in all, to recite the Lotus Sutra, and expounded it for them. When I came to the chapter The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa, I suddenly understood the Buddha's meaning: it is to point out that for everyone in this Saha world what lies before their eyes is just the Huazang realm. But the need for the three transformations was solely for those of inferior faculties, gradually revealing a glimpse. So I wrote A Tap on the Measure of the Lotus Sutra. Youwu was impetuous and fierce by nature, full of generous ardor; he knew to respect monks but did not know the Buddhadharma. When he was about to return home I saw him off on his boat and applied the tongs and hammer heavily. He was suddenly and utterly awakened, and I gave him the style Layman Juefei and showed him an inscription, and also wrote the Inscription on Clearing the Mind to warn him. (The censor Fan Youxuan, once. Zhou Haimen, that is, the former Dingshi, a second time. Long Zhang, Wang Anshun, Feng Changli, and the disciples Xingrong, Rugan, Tong'an, and Chaoyi, once each. Master Da, four times. Ding Youwu, three times.)

Zheng knows: praying for the heir, obtaining the heir, establishing the heir, contending over the heir — all are one and the same criminal case, one and the same matter of the heart. Therefore he makes a point, for Lord Fan's distant exile, of bringing out the scenery of Leiyang, and there is a deep feeling in it throughout. Then he says suddenly, I often recalled Master Da's vow concerning the sutra — he had not forgotten the mind with which he vowed to recite the Lotus Sutra a hundred times. And so, preaching the Dharma for Leiyang, he wrote A Tap on the Measure of the Lotus Sutra; that is its origin. The Outer Record says: the eye of the teachings and the eye of the Chan lineage are from the first not two eyes. Master Yongming, in setting forth the lineage, drew entirely on the words of the teachings to seal and confirm it, fearing that people would go astray along the road of no-meaning. If one does not gain the eye of the teachings, one falls into wrong views. My annotations of the Diamond, Lotus, Lankavatara, Surangama, and other sutras all pick out what bursts forth where feeling and consciousness cannot reach and where the road of no-meaning is cut off. Thus one seals the lineage with the teachings; students should gain it for themselves.

Zheng reflects that Hanshan, in bringing his disciples to accomplishment, applied the tongs and hammer without stint, prescribing medicine according to the illness and turning them suddenly to awakening. Men like Ding Youwu cannot be counted on more than one hand's fingers. For though many followed him, most were shallow admirers. If one examines throughout the chronicle the points to which he gave his mind, they can be numbered as clearly as by lamplight. The Inscription on Clearing the Mind says: The true nature, deep and still, is like water settled clear; when hate and love strike it, affliction's waves appear. Wave upon wave, unceasing, the self-nature turns opaque; affliction and ignorance but deeper unawareness make. To take the other with the self is mud cast into water; to let the other stir the self is oil upon the fire. The other troubles my truth, yet the trouble is my own; if I do not arise, the kalpa's fire freezes to stone. Therefore the perfected man first empties the mark of self; if self is empty, from what can the other obstruct him? The work of forgetting self lies in unshaken patience; the moment habit-energy stirs, wake with sudden vehemence. Where you wake, there is awakening; one thought turns back the light. Sweep away all traces, cut off every footstep's print — instantly cool and clear, still, silent, standing straight, tranquil and calm, gladdening the spirit: nothing can oppose it.

Afterwards the Caoxi Gazetteer was completed in four fascicles, with prefaces and postscripts by Chen Dake of the supreme command, the vice-minister Yang Qiyuan, the grand counselor Zhou Rudeng, and the military commissioner Hou Jigao.
The Twenty-Seventh Year, Jihai ●

I was fifty-four. In spring the printing of the Lankavatara Notes was completed. I expounded it once for the assembly, then had more than a hundred copies printed and sent them everywhere to men of knowledge in the Dharma gate throughout the land, and to the magistrates who protected the Dharma, that they might know that in the midst of adversity I had not forgotten the Buddha's work. I also feared that if I died unheard of, I should leave words to show my purpose and hope to hand down something imperishable. There were those who did not understand and thought me presumptuous. The customs of Guangdong were indeed fond of killing; at the Zhongyuan festival all slaughtered animals to sacrifice to the dead, and at that time the market piled up livestock like firewood — a pitiful sight. So I held a Yulanpen assembly, expounded the Filial Piety Commentary, and urged people on that day to feed monks, release living creatures, and use vegetarian offerings; many followed. From then on, for all great matters of funeral and sacrifice, or on parents' birthdays, whether prayers for blessing or repentance rites, they released life and ate vegetarian. Before long, life-release assemblies appeared everywhere — one of the turning points by which the Buddhadharma transformed the region. At that time the Huizhou vice-minister Lord Yang Fusuo had long had a deep Dharma affinity with me and had returned home for mourning. That autumn I went to visit him; on the day I arrived the lord had already died at his mourning lodge, and the next morning, as I was about to enter the mountains, his coffin had already reached the city. I went at once to attend the dressing of the body, and sought a coffin and an outer coffin to see him properly laid to rest. It happened that Lord Ren, circuit intendant of Chaoyang, was accompanying the imperial inspector at Huiyang and invited me to tour West Lake. I climbed Dongpo's White Crane Peak and returned, with a song; on returning I wished only to shut my door and sweep away the dust. (The Huizhou vice-minister Lord Yang Fusuo and Lord Ren, circuit intendant of Chaoyang, once each. Lord Yang was named Qiyuan; Lord Ren was named Kerong.)

Zheng's note: West Lake at Huizhou and West Lake at Hangzhou are two scenic legacies of Dongpo, and Hanshan made surpassing karmic ties at both. Zheng himself had the good fortune only at the Hangzhou lake, where he took part in the life-release assembly. Note also that Lord Yang Fusuo wrote the preface to the Caoxi Gazetteer for Hanshan; their Dharma bond was very deep, and he had long come to pay his respects. On the day of the visit the coffin happened to arrive — this too was a turning of Dharma affinity, and no mere accident.
The Twenty-Eighth Year, Gengzi ●

I was fifty-five. At that time the tax commissioners had just been sent out, and the region was shaken; added to this were alarms of Japanese pirates, and men's hearts were in a panic. I therefore dismissed my disciples and shut myself away out of sight to avoid it all. The Cantonese had long suffered from the white-sailed boats of the Fujian sea carrying rice, fearing that prices would soar, and at that time they took it as a cause of disorder. The new military commissioner was a man of Fujian, and his son's boat was anchored at sea. Just then the Grand General had asked leave and was about to depart; the tax commissioner, who was nursing designs against him, happened to find several white-sailed boats and used them as a pretext that the Grand General was providing passage for the young lord. He incited the townspeople, and there was a great uproar. In a moment several thousand gathered, hurling bricks and stones, attacking the young lord's boat until it nearly broke apart, and besieging the general's headquarters with weapons leveled; the situation was acute. Just then the three provincial offices and the prefectural and county officials had all gone to Duanzhou to perform the festival ceremonies, and there was not a single ranking official in the provincial city — no one at all to rescue the situation, and the turn of events hung on a breath. The Grand General was in peril; at his wit's end he ordered his central army commander to come before my gate to beg for help. I firmly refused, saying: 'I have no magic art.' The commander knelt in tears and said: 'If you, master, will not think of my general, will you not think of the living beings of this region?' Hearing this I was struck with alarm, and there was no help for it, so I opened my gate and went to see the tax commissioner, calmly persuading and transforming him and opening his understanding. When the commissioner heard my words he indeed awoke, and ordered that the people be pacified by his own proclamation, so dispersing the rioters. I had gone on ahead and spoken boldly to the crowd: 'What you want now is to eat cheap rice. But you are now breaking the great law and will be put to death. Even if there is cheap rice, who will eat it?' The crowd was stunned. Presently the order arrived, the siege of the general's headquarters was lifted, and the provincial city was at peace. The elders were grateful to me and wished to make offerings in my honor as to a departed spirit. At that time the three provincial offices were dining at the commissioner's yamen; when the report came that the people were rioting they all threw down their chopsticks and rose, and by the time they returned all was already quiet. Yet they all understood my intention. When Lord Ren, the circuit intendant, heard of it, he wrote to me: 'If Master Hanshan had not come out, what would have become of the region? Now that Master Hanshan has come out, what is to become of Master Hanshan?' I too knew that from then on there would be no peaceful days. In the seventh month of autumn Lord Zhu Xingcun, circuit intendant of Nan-Shao, invited me to Caoxi. I took him at his word and went into the mountains, becoming a slave of the Sixth Patriarch. At that time the new supreme commander Lord Dai, learning that I had pacified the rioters, was deeply grateful and wished to meet me, and instructed the Grand General to bring me. I went to him; at the meeting his courtesy was most generous, and he kept me to a vegetarian feast. When I begged leave to go to Caoxi, the lord was pleased to become a protector of the Dharma, and told me to report to him if anything arose, and only then could I set my mind at ease. (The Grand General, whose surname is unknown, a second time. The tax commissioner, once. Intendant Ren, a second time. Lord Zhu Xingcun, intendant of Nan-Shao, and the new supreme commander Lord Dai, once each. Lord Zhu was named Yibin, a native of Haining, and served as prefect of Yingtianfu. Lord Dai was named Yao.)

Zheng wonders at this Grand General: he appears twice in the chronicle, with no surname or title. Could it be that he only knew to honor a famous monk and did not know how to wield authority and trust in the region, so that a single provocation nearly became a great upheaval, and he had no choice but to rely on a teacher of goodness to lend a hand? A single phrase awakened the tax commissioner and dispersed the rioters. The old courtesy of loosing his bonds and offering a vegetarian meal — how heavily it was repaid! The way he settled the trouble that day — how it came off in a snap of the fingers, as if divine! Afterwards those in office, hearing the wind, rose up, and from that time Caoxi began to shine.
The Twenty-Ninth Year, Xinchou ●

I was fifty-six. In the first month of spring I saw vagabonds from all quarters gathered at the mountain gate, opening butcher stalls and wine shops, exceedingly foul, a long-standing abuse of more than a hundred years. Graves routinely encroached on the Patriarch's mountain, and monks' property was much encroached upon. They colluded with outside ruffians to extort and swindle, and none of the temple monks dared look them in the face. I sighed and said: 'This is a disease in the heart and belly. If it is not removed, the Sixth Patriarch's seat of practice will in the end become a fox's den, past all saving. What is to be done? There is no way to deal with it. Though I stay here, what use am I?' After long deliberation, having no alternative, I went to inform the supreme commander Lord Dai. The lord said: 'There is no difficulty. I will try to carry it through for you.' He at once ordered the county to take up station and within three days drive them all out, not leaving a single man, and to tear down every shop and stall, not leaving a tile. From then on the accumulated filth of Caoxi's mountain gate was washed clean in a single day. The lord then kept me to a vegetarian meal, and in the course of conversation said: 'I have washed away the stench from the Sixth Patriarch for you. But now the living beings of this region are in misery — what compassion has the great bodhisattva to save them?' I asked what he meant. The lord said: 'The thousand pearl boats are almost all great pirates of the sea. Now, under cover of the imperial pearl fishery, they are given power; when the fishery ends they do not return but run wild at sea, plundering without end, and the law cannot stop them. That is one thing. As for the mines opened in the region, the conscripted laborers are violent and overbearing, digging up people's graves and ruining their property; everywhere the common people suffer their poison, worse than plunder, so that none can sleep in peace. What is to be done about it?' I said: 'This is not easy to speak of; let us plan it slowly.' The pearl commissioner Lord Li had considerable faith. That autumn he came to Caoxi to offer incense to the Sixth Patriarch and stayed in the mountains several days, greatly delighted to hear the Dharma. I therefore urged him to be the golden donor for the revival of the ancestral court, and he generously undertook it with all his strength. I quietly suggested to him: 'The harm that mining does to the region is very great, and it is not the sage emperor's intent. As for the pearl boats, set limits and deadlines at once, and punish those who exceed them in coming and going. As for the mines, stop the digging, withdraw all the conscripted laborers, and simply require the responsible offices to send in the annual quota, without the slightest disturbance to the people — would that be possible?' The commissioner assented and carried it out with all his strength. Thus the coastal and mountain region was at peace in a single day. The lord was deeply grateful and wrote to thank me: 'Now at last I know the breadth of the Buddha and Patriarchs' compassion.' From this his resolve to protect the Dharma grew ever firmer. Because of this I was able to set my mind at ease at Caoxi, open up the ancestral court, redirect the feng shui and the roads, select monks and confer precepts, establish a charity school, nurture novices, set up a treasury office and pure rules, audit the land rents, redeem monks' property, and recover what had been encroached upon. In a single year a hundred neglected works were all set in order. (Lord Dai of the supreme command, a second time. Commissioner Li of the pearl fishery, once.)
